questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design architectures built for the cloud
questions.question: A retailer split its order monolith into microservices, and the inventory service now consumes order events from an Amazon SQS standard queue. During a recent sale, a few malformed messages failed on every attempt and kept reappearing, tying up consumers while healthy orders waited. The same week, a downstream supplier API throttled requests for several minutes, causing many valid messages to fail temporarily. Messages that fail on every attempt must be set aside for later analysis so they stop consuming capacity meant for healthy orders. Valid messages that fail because of short downstream throttling must still be retried several times before they are set aside. Which change best meets both requirements?
options: Attach a dead-letter queue through a redrive policy and set maxReceiveCount high enough to allow several retries first.
Raise the queue visibility timeout so consumers keep retrying each failed message for longer before other consumers see it.
Move the workload to a FIFO queue so each failed message is retried in order until processing finally succeeds.
Attach a dead-letter queue through a redrive policy and set maxReceiveCount to one so failures move out at once.
questions.correct_rationale: A dead-letter queue sets poison messages aside, and a higher maxReceiveCount leaves room for retries during short throttling.
distractor_rationales: A longer visibility timeout changes retry timing but never sets poison messages aside, so they keep consuming capacity.
A FIFO queue retrying until success lets one poison message block the group behind it and sets nothing aside.
Poison messages are set aside, but a single receive moves throttled valid messages out before any retry.
questions.distractor_summary: WA moves messages after one failure; WB only delays retries; X blocks on poison messages.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design architectures built for the cloud
questions.question: A media company enriches metadata for millions of image objects in Amazon S3 every night. Today a script on one large EC2 instance walks the bucket sequentially and regularly runs past the nightly window, and when it crashes nobody can tell which objects were processed. The enrichment must fan out across many objects at the same time so the whole run finishes inside the nightly window. The team wants serverless orchestration with tracking of each item's success or failure, and it will not operate a server fleet. Which design should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Build a Step Functions workflow whose Map state in Inline mode iterates over every object within the parent workflow execution.
Invoke one Lambda function each night that lists the bucket and processes each object in a loop before it exits.
Build a Step Functions workflow whose Map state in Distributed mode iterates over the objects and runs child workflows in parallel.
Run an Auto Scaling group of EC2 workers that pull object keys from an Amazon SQS queue and process them in parallel.
questions.correct_rationale: Distributed mode is built for large-scale parallel processing of S3 data and tracks each child workflow, with no servers to operate.
distractor_rationales: Inline mode stays serverless, but it runs iterations inside one parent execution and is not the large-scale parallel mode.
One sequential Lambda invocation gives no fan-out and cannot finish millions of objects in a single run.
The worker fleet runs in parallel, but the team must operate EC2 servers and build its own per-item tracking.
questions.distractor_summary: WA needs a server fleet; WB uses Inline mode; X processes sequentially.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design architectures built for the cloud
questions.question: A company runs several dozen workload accounts in AWS Organizations, and the central operations team must react to order-failure events emitted by applications in every account. Accounts are created through an account vending process almost every week, and the operations team has repeatedly missed events from new accounts. Accounts that join the organization later must be able to deliver events without anyone editing the central configuration for each account. Events must reach the operations account as they occur, without polling jobs or periodic exports. What should the solutions architect implement?
options: Create a central event bus whose resource policy grants the organization, with rules in workload accounts that target that bus.
Have each workload account export application events to a shared S3 bucket that the operations account processes on a schedule.
Run a central Lambda function that assumes a role in each account and polls its CloudTrail events every few minutes.
Create a central event bus whose resource policy lists each workload account ID, and append new IDs as accounts are created.
questions.correct_rationale: Granting the organization in the bus policy admits new accounts automatically, and rules deliver events as they happen.
distractor_rationales: A bucket shared through an organization condition can admit new accounts, but scheduled processing is not delivery as events occur.
Polling CloudTrail through assumed roles is the polling design ruled out, and each new account needs a role.
Events arrive in near real time, but the bus policy must be edited for every new account.
questions.distractor_summary: WA needs per-account policy edits; WB is scheduled; X polls.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.2 Integrate AI and ML services into architectures
questions.question: An insurer wants an internal assistant that answers adjuster questions from policy wording and claims guidelines stored as documents in Amazon S3. Legal updates a portion of these documents every week, and the assistant must cite the current version when it answers. Answers must reflect the documents as they stand each week without retraining or customizing a model after every update. The team wants a managed retrieval capability instead of building and operating its own embedding and vector search pipeline. Which approach should the solutions architect choose?
options: Load every policy document into the prompt of each request so the model reads the complete library for every answer.
Fine-tune a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock on the policy documents each week and serve answers from the tuned model.
Build a Lambda pipeline that embeds each changed document and stores vectors in a search cluster the team runs on EC2.
Create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over the S3 documents, sync it after updates, and generate answers from retrieved passages.
questions.correct_rationale: A knowledge base retrieves relevant passages from current documents at query time and is managed, so no weekly model retraining is needed.
distractor_rationales: Placing the whole library in every prompt does not scale and still provides no managed retrieval of relevant passages.
Weekly fine-tuning is managed, but it customizes the model after every update and does not retrieve source passages.
Self-built embeddings can reflect current documents, but the team must operate the pipeline and vector search cluster.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is self-operated; WB retrains weekly; X stuffs the prompt.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.2 Integrate AI and ML services into architectures
questions.question: A European bank runs a customer service assistant on Amazon Bedrock in one EU Region. At month-end peaks, on-demand requests are throttled and response times spike, but traffic is low for the rest of the month, so the finance team rejects any long-term capacity purchase for a few peak days. The application must absorb the month-end bursts without buying dedicated model capacity for the whole month. Regulators require that inference for these customers is processed inside EU geographic boundaries. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Call the model through an EU geographic cross-Region inference profile so requests are routed among Regions within the EU.
Call the model through a global cross-Region inference profile so requests can be served from Regions anywhere in the world.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model in the existing EU Region and route all assistant traffic to that capacity.
Add client-side retries with exponential backoff and jitter so throttled requests are resubmitted to the same EU Region.
questions.correct_rationale: An EU geographic profile spreads bursts across EU Regions on demand while keeping processing inside EU boundaries.
distractor_rationales: A global profile absorbs bursts, but requests can be processed outside the EU, which breaks the residency requirement.
Provisioned Throughput keeps processing in the EU, but it buys dedicated capacity the bank does not want for a few peak days.
Retries spread load over time but add no capacity, so bursts still throttle and response times stay high.
questions.distractor_summary: WA leaves the EU; WB buys capacity; X adds no capacity.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design hybrid cloud integration patterns
questions.question: A manufacturing plant runs line-control applications that write quality images to an on-premises NAS over NFS. The NAS is near end of life, and the company wants plant data in AWS so analysts can apply lifecycle rules and run analytics on it, while the plant keeps working through short WAN slowdowns. The plant applications must keep writing over NFS with no code changes. The data must land as Amazon S3 objects so lifecycle policies and analytics tools can use it directly. Which solution should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Replace the NAS with an Amazon EFS file system that the plant servers mount over NFS through the WAN link.
Deploy Amazon S3 File Gateway at the plant and present an NFS file share backed by an S3 bucket.
Change the plant applications to upload images straight to Amazon S3 through the SDK and retire the NAS share.
Deploy a Volume Gateway in cached mode at the plant and present iSCSI volumes to the plant servers.
questions.correct_rationale: S3 File Gateway keeps an NFS share for the applications and stores the files as S3 objects with local caching.
distractor_rationales: EFS keeps NFS, but the data lives in a file system rather than as S3 objects for lifecycle rules.
Direct SDK uploads produce S3 objects, but they require changing the plant applications.
Volume Gateway presents block volumes over iSCSI, so applications lose the NFS share and files are not S3 objects.
questions.distractor_summary: WA changes code; WB is not S3; X is block storage.

questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design hybrid cloud integration patterns
questions.question: A company connects its data center to a shared services VPC over AWS Direct Connect. Applications in AWS use private hosted zones, while corporate systems such as directory and ticketing are named under a domain served by on-premises DNS servers. The network team will not run DNS server software on EC2 instances. On-premises servers must resolve names in the private hosted zones used by the AWS applications. Applications in the VPCs must resolve names in the corporate domain served by the on-premises DNS servers. Which configuration meets both requirements?
options: Create an inbound Resolver endpoint for on-premises queries and an outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for the corporate domain.
Run BIND forwarders on EC2 instances in the shared services VPC and point both environments at those forwarders.
Create an inbound Resolver endpoint and configure the on-premises DNS servers to forward private hosted zone queries to it.
Create an outbound Resolver endpoint with a forwarding rule that sends corporate domain queries to the on-premises servers.
questions.correct_rationale: Inbound endpoints answer queries from on-premises, and an outbound endpoint with a rule forwards corporate queries out.
distractor_rationales: BIND forwarders on EC2 could work, but the team has ruled out running DNS server software on instances.
The inbound endpoint covers on-premises lookups, but VPC applications still cannot resolve the corporate domain.
The outbound rule covers corporate lookups from VPCs, but on-premises servers still cannot reach private hosted zones.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is inbound only; WB is outbound only; X runs DNS servers on EC2.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.4 Design network architectures
questions.question: A company has a transit gateway in a US Region and another in an EU Region, each attached to dozens of VPCs. A new analytics platform in the EU must reach databases in several US VPCs, and more VPCs on both sides will need the same connectivity over time. The design must not require a separate peering connection between every pair of VPCs as the estate grows. Traffic between the Regions must stay on the AWS network and must not depend on VPN tunnels over the internet. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?
options: Create inter-Region VPC peering connections between each EU VPC and each US VPC that must reach the databases.
Peer the two transit gateways, accept the attachment, and add static routes in each route table to the peering attachment.
Create Site-to-Site VPN attachments between the two transit gateways and exchange routes dynamically with BGP over the tunnels.
Peer the two transit gateways and turn on route propagation so each side learns the other's VPC routes automatically.
questions.correct_rationale: Transit gateway peering avoids pairwise VPC peering and uses AWS infrastructure, with static routes to the attachment.
distractor_rationales: Inter-Region VPC peering stays on AWS infrastructure, but it needs a connection for every VPC pair.
VPN attachments avoid pairwise peering, but the tunnels run over the internet, which breaks the second requirement.
Peering is right, but routes across a peering attachment are added as static routes rather than learned by propagation.
questions.distractor_summary: WA relies on propagation; WB uses internet VPN; X builds a mesh.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.4 Design network architectures
questions.question: A platform team in a central account runs an internal pricing API that dozens of business unit accounts consume. Today the business unit VPCs reach it through broad network links, and an audit found that consumers could also reach unrelated databases in the platform VPC. Consumers must be able to reach the pricing API but not any other resources in the platform VPC. Traffic must stay private, with no internet gateways, NAT devices, or VPN connections in the path. Which design best meets these requirements?
options: Front the API with a Network Load Balancer as an endpoint service, and have consumers create interface VPC endpoints for it.
Peer the platform VPC with each consumer VPC and rely on security groups in the platform VPC to limit consumer access.
Attach every consumer VPC and the platform VPC to a transit gateway that shares one route table across all attachments.
Publish the API through an internet-facing Application Load Balancer and allow requests from the consumers' NAT addresses alone.
questions.correct_rationale: An endpoint service exposes the API alone through interface endpoints, and traffic needs no internet, NAT, or VPN path.
distractor_rationales: Peering is private, but it opens routing to the whole platform VPC and relies on every security group being correct.
A shared transit gateway route table is private, but it gives consumers network paths to the entire platform VPC.
Allow lists can narrow exposure to the API, but the traffic crosses the internet through NAT devices.
questions.distractor_summary: WA and X open whole-VPC routing; WB crosses the internet.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.4 Design network architectures
questions.question: A company has one AWS Direct Connect connection at a US location that serves VPCs in the nearest Region. It is now launching workloads in two more Regions, including one in Europe, and the data center must reach all of them privately. The company wants to reuse its existing Direct Connect connection rather than ordering new connections near each Region. Traffic to the new Regions must not travel over the internet, including through encrypted tunnels. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create Site-to-Site VPN connections from the data center to virtual private gateways in each new Region over the internet.
Create a Direct Connect gateway on the existing connection and associate it with the gateways for VPCs in each Region.
Order a new Direct Connect connection at a location near each new Region and attach each one to that Region's VPCs.
Keep the private virtual interface to the nearest Region and use VPC peering to reach VPCs in the other Regions.
questions.correct_rationale: A Direct Connect gateway reaches VPCs in any Region from the existing connection without using the internet.
distractor_rationales: VPN tunnels reuse no new circuits, but they cross the internet, which the company has ruled out.
New connections keep traffic private, but they replace the reuse of the existing connection the company wants.
VPC peering is not transitive, so on-premises traffic cannot pass through one VPC to reach peered VPCs.
questions.distractor_summary: WA orders new circuits; WB uses the internet; X relies on transitive peering.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.5 Design data, storage, and database architectures
questions.question: A brokerage runs its account service on Amazon Aurora MySQL in a US Region. Users in Europe and Asia report slow account pages, and the risk committee has asked for recovery from a Regional outage within minutes. The application must stay on MySQL-compatible SQL with no schema redesign. Users in Europe and Asia need low-latency reads served from copies of the data close to them. The database must recover from a Regional outage within minutes using managed replication, not application-level copying. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Copy automated snapshots of the cluster to Regions in Europe and Asia and restore a new cluster during a Regional outage.
Migrate the data model to Amazon DynamoDB global tables so every Region holds a writable replica of the account data.
Convert the cluster to an Aurora global database with secondary clusters in Europe and Asia and use failover for Regional outages.
Deploy Amazon ElastiCache clusters in Europe and Asia that cache query results read from the primary Aurora cluster in the home Region.
questions.correct_rationale: Secondary clusters give nearby low-latency reads, and managed replication supports fast recovery to another Region.
distractor_rationales: Snapshot copies support Regional recovery, but restores are slow and provide no low-latency reads for remote users.
DynamoDB global tables would need a schema redesign away from MySQL-compatible SQL, which the company has ruled out.
Regional caches speed up reads, but they provide no managed database replica for recovering from a Regional outage.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is slow restore; WB is only a cache; X needs a redesign.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.5 Design data, storage, and database architectures
questions.question: A gaming company stores player profiles and inventories in a DynamoDB table in one Region. It is launching game servers in North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, and players in each region update their inventories many times per session. Game servers in every region must write player updates to a local replica rather than to a distant home Region. The company will not build or operate its own replication code between tables. Which solution should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create tables in each region and use DynamoDB Streams with Lambda functions to copy every write to the other regions.
Copy table backups to the other regions with AWS Backup every hour and restore a local table when needed.
Convert the table to a DynamoDB global table with replicas in the three regions and point game servers at their local replica.
Keep one table in the home Region and send writes from every region to it over private networking on AWS.
questions.correct_rationale: Global tables provide multi-active replicas that accept local writes and replicate them without custom code.
distractor_rationales: Streams and Lambda allow local writes, but the company would build and operate its own replication.
Hourly backup copies are not writable replicas and do not replicate live updates between regions.
A single home table needs no replication code, but writes from distant regions are not local.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is custom replication; WB writes remotely; X is backups.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design identity security architectures
questions.question: An enterprise with more than a hundred AWS accounts manages its workforce in Microsoft Entra ID. Database administrators need the same administrative access in about thirty accounts, and today each account has its own IAM users for them, which auditors have flagged. The database administrator permissions must be defined once and reused across all the target accounts. Administrators must sign in with their corporate identities, and no IAM users may be created for them. Which solution should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Connect IAM Identity Center to Entra ID and assign one database administrator permission set to the group across the target accounts.
Deploy an IAM role to each target account with StackSets and let administrators switch into it from IAM users in one account.
Create an Amazon Cognito user pool federated with Entra ID and grant database administrator access through its groups.
Configure a SAML identity provider in each target account for Entra ID and maintain a separate administrator role definition per account.
questions.correct_rationale: A permission set is defined once and assigned across accounts, and Entra ID identities sign in with no IAM users.
distractor_rationales: StackSets reuse one role definition, but administrators still sign in through IAM users, which auditors flagged.
Cognito user pools serve application users and do not assign AWS account access to workforce groups.
Per-account SAML uses corporate identities, but each account keeps its own role definition to maintain.
questions.distractor_summary: WA keeps IAM users; WB is per-account; X is for app users.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design identity security architectures
questions.question: A research company runs a shared analytics account where dozens of project teams each own their own S3 prefixes, DynamoDB tables, and Lambda functions. Projects start and finish every month, and the security team edits a growing set of per-project IAM policies by hand. Last quarter a policy edit was missed and a contractor kept access to a closed project for several weeks. Starting a new project must not require writing or editing any IAM policy, so the policy count stays flat as projects grow. A person must reach a project's resources solely while their identity carries that project's attribute, so removing the attribute ends access. Which approach should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create one permission set per project in IAM Identity Center and assign it to the project's group when each new project starts.
Use a permissions boundary on each user that lists the resource ARNs of every project the user is permitted to reach today.
Create one IAM role per project with a policy listing that project's resource ARNs, and add a role whenever a project starts.
Tag principals and resources with a project key and write a few policies that allow actions when the two tag values match.
questions.correct_rationale: Matching principal and resource tags lets a fixed set of policies cover new projects, and removing the principal tag ends access.
distractor_rationales: Per-project permission sets still grow with each project and need a new assignment for every project start.
Boundaries listing resource ARNs must be edited for every project change, which is the manual work being removed.
Per-project roles keep access scoped, but every new project needs another role and resource list.
questions.distractor_summary: WA and WB grow per project; X needs manual ARN edits.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design identity security architectures
questions.question: A manufacturer is midway through a two-year migration, and several on-premises batch servers upload production data to S3 every hour. Each server holds an IAM user access key that was created years ago, and an internal audit found two keys copied into a shared wiki page. The company already runs an enterprise certificate authority that issues X.509 certificates to every managed server. Long-term access keys must be removed from the on-premises servers so a copied secret cannot be reused indefinitely. The servers must keep uploading to S3 without a network redesign or a new hardware appliance in the data center. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Deploy an S3 File Gateway appliance in the data center and have the servers write files to its local share instead.
Move the access keys into AWS Secrets Manager and have each server fetch its IAM user key from Secrets Manager at startup.
Rotate each IAM user access key on a monthly schedule with a script and store the new keys in an encrypted file.
Set up IAM Roles Anywhere with the company CA as a trust anchor so servers get temporary credentials from certificates.
questions.correct_rationale: Roles Anywhere trusts the existing certificate authority and returns temporary credentials, so no long-term key remains on servers.
distractor_rationales: A gateway appliance adds new data center hardware or a VM, and the gateway still needs credentials of its own.
Fetching the key from Secrets Manager still needs a credential on the server, and the user key remains long-term.
Rotation shortens key life, but long-term keys still sit on servers and a copied key works until rotated.
questions.distractor_summary: WA keeps long-term keys; WB adds an appliance; X still stores a user key.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design solutions to implement encryption and key management strategies
questions.question: A payments company encrypts card tokens in its application with AWS KMS before writing them to a DynamoDB global table that replicates to a second Region. During a regional failover test, the application in the recovery Region could read the replicated items but could not decrypt the tokens, because each was encrypted under a single-Region key in the primary Region. Applications in the recovery Region must decrypt replicated ciphertext even when the primary Region is fully unavailable. The data must not be re-encrypted during replication, and decryption must not depend on a call back to the primary Region. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create a separate single-Region key in the recovery Region and re-encrypt each token with it before items replicate there.
Import identical key material into two unrelated single-Region keys and let the application choose a key by its Region.
Keep the single-Region key and have the recovery application call AWS KMS in the primary Region to decrypt each token.
Encrypt with a multi-Region primary key and create a replica key in the recovery Region that shares the same key material.
questions.correct_rationale: A replica multi-Region key holds the same key material and key ID, so recovery-Region apps decrypt locally without re-encryption.
distractor_rationales: A local key in the recovery Region works, but tokens must be re-encrypted during replication, which is ruled out.
Unrelated keys with imported material have different key IDs, so ciphertext from one is not recognized by the other.
Calling KMS in the primary Region fails when that Region is unavailable, which is the scenario being designed for.
questions.distractor_summary: WA re-encrypts; WB depends on the primary Region; X yields different key IDs.

docLinks.title: Multi-Region keys in AWS KMS

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design solutions to implement encryption and key management strategies
questions.question: A telemetry platform writes billions of small objects per month to an S3 data lake that must use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key for compliance. The finance team found that AWS KMS request charges now exceed the storage cost of the bucket, and the platform team has seen KMS request throttling during ingestion peaks. Objects must stay encrypted with SSE-KMS under the same customer managed key so the compliance control does not change. The volume of requests that S3 sends to AWS KMS must drop sharply without changing how producers write objects. Which change should the solutions architect make?
options: Switch the bucket to SSE-S3 managed keys so encryption no longer generates any AWS KMS requests from Amazon S3.
Request a higher AWS KMS request quota so ingestion peaks stop throttling while each object still calls AWS KMS.
Enable an S3 Bucket Key on the bucket so S3 uses a bucket-level key and makes far fewer requests to AWS KMS.
Have producers encrypt each object on the client with a data key before upload and store objects without SSE-KMS.
questions.correct_rationale: A Bucket Key keeps SSE-KMS under the same customer managed key and cuts the number of KMS requests from S3.
distractor_rationales: SSE-S3 removes KMS requests but drops the customer managed key that the compliance control requires.
A higher quota eases throttling but leaves request volume and KMS charges unchanged.
Client-side encryption changes how producers write and drops SSE-KMS, breaking both stated requirements.
questions.distractor_summary: WA drops the managed key; WB keeps request volume; X changes producers.

docLinks.title: Reducing the cost of SSE-KMS with Amazon S3 Bucket Keys

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Design multi-account governance and compliance solutions
questions.question: A holding company attached an SCP at the organization root that denies disabling AWS CloudTrail. A later review found that an engineer stopped a trail by using an administrator role in the management account, where several legacy workloads still run. The security team wants the CloudTrail guardrail to hold for every workload, including those legacy workloads. The guardrail must apply to every principal that runs workloads, so no workload team can stop the organization trail. Changes must keep the organization structure intact and must not depend on each workload team writing its own deny policy. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Move the legacy workloads from the management account into member accounts under the root, where the existing SCP applies to them.
Ask each workload team to add an explicit deny for stopping trails to its own IAM roles in the management account.
Add a permissions boundary to every administrator role in the management account so stopping the trail falls outside it.
Attach the CloudTrail deny SCP directly to the management account as well so it governs the administrator roles there.
questions.correct_rationale: SCPs do not affect principals in the management account, so moving workloads into member accounts brings them under the guardrail.
distractor_rationales: Team-written denies depend on each workload team, which the requirement rules out, and admins can remove them.
Boundaries in the management account rely on its administrators, who can edit or remove the boundary themselves.
Attaching the SCP to the management account has no effect, because SCPs do not affect its users or roles.
questions.distractor_summary: WA has no effect there; WB relies on teams; X is removable by admins.

docLinks.title: Service control policies (SCPs)

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Design multi-account governance and compliance solutions
questions.question: A bank runs hundreds of member accounts and must enforce a data perimeter on its S3 buckets. Teams often write bucket policies with broad grants for partner integrations, and a recent review found a bucket readable by an unknown external account. SCPs are already in place, but they govern requests made by the bank's own principals. Principals from outside the organization must be blocked from reaching S3 buckets in member accounts, whatever each bucket policy grants. The control must be set centrally once and must not rely on every team rewriting its existing bucket policies correctly. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?
options: Attach a resource control policy at the root that denies S3 access when the requesting principal is outside the organization.
Publish a standard bucket policy template that denies external principals and ask each team to apply it to its buckets.
Add a statement to the existing SCPs that denies S3 access when the requesting principal belongs to an external account.
Enable IAM Access Analyzer in each account and have teams remove external grants from their bucket policies when findings appear.
questions.correct_rationale: An RCP limits what external principals can do with resources in member accounts, centrally and regardless of bucket grants.
distractor_rationales: A template depends on every team applying it correctly, which the requirement rules out.
SCPs govern the organization's own principals, so a deny there does not stop requests from external accounts.
Access Analyzer finds external grants, but removal waits on each team and nothing blocks access first.
questions.distractor_summary: WA governs own principals; WB relies on teams; X detects after the fact.

docLinks.title: Resource control policies (RCPs)

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Design multi-account governance and compliance solutions
questions.question: A European insurer runs its accounts in an AWS Control Tower landing zone with separate OUs for production, development, and sandboxes. A regulator requires customer data to remain in approved Regions, and the platform lead asked for Region restriction on the production OU while sandboxes stay open. An architect proposes turning on the landing-zone Region deny setting, AWS-GR_REGION_DENY, from the Landing zone settings page for this purpose. Workloads must be blocked from using Regions outside the approved set in a way the regulator can see as a managed control. The team must understand where the AWS-GR_REGION_DENY landing-zone setting takes effect before it promises any OU-level difference. Which statement about the proposal is correct?
options: The landing-zone Region deny setting is applied to individual accounts, so each production account is enrolled with it separately.
The landing-zone Region deny setting applies to the whole landing zone, so sandbox OUs are restricted along with production.
The landing-zone Region deny setting is enabled per OU, so the platform team can restrict production and leave sandboxes open.
The landing-zone Region deny setting is a detective control that reports usage in other Regions without blocking requests.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS-GR_REGION_DENY applies to the landing zone as a whole, so the proposal cannot restrict production alone.
distractor_rationales: AWS-GR_REGION_DENY is not an account-by-account control; it covers the landing zone as a whole.

Per-account roles give no single view, and console roles may allow changes in source accounts.

Replace all Spot capacity with On-Demand Instances in the Auto Scaling group so that no worker is ever interrupted.
Switch the group's Spot allocation strategy to capacity optimized and stop considering price when selecting Spot pools.

Create an S3 interface endpoint in each private subnet and point the Spark jobs at the endpoint-specific DNS names for S3.
Create an S3 gateway endpoint and add it to the private subnet route tables so S3 traffic bypasses the NAT gateways.

NAT instances avoid the managed NAT fee but still route S3 traffic through an operated NAT device.
Interface endpoints also bypass NAT, but they add hourly and data processing charges that the second requirement rules out.

CloudFront can cut origin load, but the institute's account still pays for the distribution traffic.

questions.subdomain: 3.4 Optimize storage and database costs

Store the documents in S3 Intelligent-Tiering with its optional archive access tiers left off, so tiering stays automatic.
Keep every document in S3 Standard and run a monthly Athena report so the legal team can archive quiet cases by hand.
Keep the lifecycle rule to S3 Standard-IA and lengthen its age threshold so fewer documents move before cases reopen.

distractor_rationales: Glacier Flexible Retrieval adds restore delays and retrieval costs when litigation begins.
Manual archiving depends on predicting quiet cases, which the first requirement rules out.
A longer threshold still guesses access by age, and reopened cases still pay Standard-IA retrieval charges.

Enable a time to live attribute that deletes trip items after a year and keep the table in the Standard table class.

An S3 export with Athena adds a pipeline and changes the query path and latency the app depends on.
Time to live deletes trip history that disputes and receipts still need.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Design migration strategies by using AWS frameworks
questions.question: A retailer must leave its colocation facility within nine months and plans to rehost about four hundred Windows and Linux servers onto EC2 without code changes. Refactor each application into containers on Amazon ECS and redeploy them through a CI/CD pipeline before the exit date.
Use AWS Transform MGN to replicate each source server at block level continuously and launch cutover instances per wave.
Use AWS DMS to migrate the databases on each server and rebuild the application tiers by hand on new EC2 instances.
questions.correct_rationale: MGN replicates servers continuously at block level and converts them for launch, keeping cutover windows short.
distractor_rationales: One-time image exports capture a point in time, so changes after export require a long outage to resync.
Refactoring into containers rewrites applications, which the first requirement rules out.
DMS moves databases, but rebuilding application tiers by hand is the manual work being avoided.

questions.question: A travel company is moving a multi-terabyte Oracle order database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL after converting its schema with the schema conversion tooling. Use AWS DataSync to copy the Oracle data files to Amazon S3 and load them into Aurora PostgreSQL from S3 later.
Run an AWS DMS task that performs a full load and then continues with change data capture until cutover.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Design disaster recovery architectures

Use Route 53 failover routing with health checks so traffic stays on the main load balancer until it fails them.
Create Route 53 latency records for both load balancers so users reach whichever Region gives them the lowest latency.
Create a simple Route 53 record for the primary load balancer and edit it by hand when an outage begins.

distractor_rationales: Equal weights split users across both Regions while both are healthy, which the second requirement rules out.
Latency routing serves users from both Regions by proximity, not from the primary alone.
Manual record edits are not automatic, which the first requirement rules out.

questions.question: A payments processor runs a stateless API on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Configure Route 53 failover records to a standby copy in a second Region and fail over whenever any single zone shows errors.
Start an ARC zonal shift away from the impaired zone and let target tracking add capacity in the healthy zones afterward.
Keep enough headroom in the Auto Scaling group for two zones, and start an ARC zonal shift away from the impaired zone.

Run AWS Fault Injection Service experiments against each application once a year and record recovery times in the spreadsheet.

A yearly experiment keeps the stale cycle that the second requirement rules out.

questions.subdomain: 5.1 Design infrastructure as code
questions.question: A retailer vends new AWS accounts into a workloads OU several times a week. Every account that joins the workloads OU must receive the baseline automatically, with no step for the platform team. Accounts moved out of the OU must have the baseline stacks removed, and the team does not want custom code to maintain. Which solution should the solutions architect implement?
options: Create a self-managed StackSet and have the platform pipeline add each new account ID to its deployment targets after vending.
Share a Service Catalog portfolio with the workloads OU so each application team launches the baseline product in its account.
Create an EventBridge rule for account creation that invokes a Lambda function to deploy the baseline stack into the account.
Create a service-managed StackSet that targets the workloads OU with automatic deployment on and stack retention turned off.

distractor_rationales: Adding account IDs is a manual pipeline step that can be forgotten, which the first requirement rules out.
Teams must launch the product themselves, so the baseline is not automatic.
A Lambda function is custom code to maintain, which the second requirement rules out.

questions.subdomain: 5.1 Design infrastructure as code
questions.question: During an outage, operators at a logistics company edited security groups and instance settings in the console across several production stacks. The next scheduled stack update is in two days, and the change board worries that it will silently overwrite or conflict with the emergency edits, but nobody recorded exactly which resources were touched. The team must find which stack resources now differ from their templates because of the console edits. Nothing in the running stacks may be changed while the investigation is under way. What should the solutions architect do first?
options: Run a stack update from the stored templates now so that every resource returns to its expected configuration.
Run CloudFormation drift detection on the affected stacks and review the resources it reports as drifted.
Create a change set for each stack from its current template and review the resources that the change set reports.
Turn on an AWS Config rule for security group ingress and review which groups it marks as noncompliant.
questions.correct_rationale: Drift detection compares actual resource configuration with the template and reports changes made outside CloudFormation.
distractor_rationales: A stack update changes running resources, which the second requirement rules out.
A change set compares the template with the stack's recorded state, not the console edits made to resources.
A Config rule checks a policy condition, not which resources differ from their stack templates.
questions.distractor_summary: WA misses console edits; WB changes resources; X checks a rule.

questions.subdomain: 5.1 Design infrastructure as code
questions.question: A fintech company deploys its production stack many times a week through a pipeline. The stack holds an RDS database alongside many application resources. Last quarter a template edit changed a database property that required replacement, and the update recreated the database from scratch, causing a long outage and a restore from backup. Stack updates must not be able to replace or delete the production database, even if a template edit would require it. Every other resource in the stack must keep updating through the pipeline without manual approval. Which control should the solutions architect add?
options: Deny cloudformation UpdateStack to the pipeline role in IAM and have an administrator run every production stack update by hand.
Set a stack policy that allows updates on all resources but denies replacement and deletion updates on the database resource.
Turn on termination protection for the production stack so that updates cannot remove or recreate the database resource.
Set a DeletionPolicy of Retain on the database resource so that a stack update keeps the database whenever it is changed.
questions.correct_rationale: A stack policy can deny replacement and deletion updates on one resource while allowing updates to everything else.
distractor_rationales: Denying UpdateStack blocks every update and adds manual steps, which the second requirement rules out.
Termination protection blocks stack deletion, not updates that replace a resource.
DeletionPolicy applies when a resource is removed or the stack is deleted, not to replacement during an update.
questions.distractor_summary: WA misses replacement; WB covers deletion of the stack; X blocks all updates.

questions.subdomain: 5.2 Design CI/CD and DevSecOps pipelines
questions.question: A travel booking company runs an HTTP API as an Amazon ECS service behind a Network Load Balancer that was chosen years ago for static IP addresses, which no partner still uses. A recent release broke checkout for every user at once. The team wants new versions to reach a small share of traffic first and roll back on alarms. Each release must send a small share of production traffic to the new task set before the rest is shifted. A CloudWatch alarm on checkout errors must roll the deployment back automatically. Keep the existing Network Load Balancer and switch the service to CodeDeploy blue/green with a canary configuration and alarm rollback.
Keep the ECS rolling update with a lower minimum healthy percent so fewer new tasks start in each release step.
Move the service behind an Application Load Balancer and use CodeDeploy blue/green with a canary configuration and alarm rollback.
questions.correct_rationale: Canary traffic shifting works with an Application Load Balancer, and CodeDeploy can roll back when a configured alarm fires.
distractor_rationales: Manual weight changes are not an automatic rollback, which the second requirement rules out.
With a Network Load Balancer, CodeDeploy supports all-at-once for ECS, so a canary shift is not available.
A rolling update replaces tasks in steps but does not hold a share of traffic or roll back on the alarm.

questions.subdomain: 5.2 Design CI/CD and DevSecOps pipelines
questions.question: A healthcare software vendor builds container images in a CodePipeline pipeline and pushes them to Amazon ECR, where enhanced scanning reports findings after each push. Twice this year an image with a critical vulnerability was deployed to production before anyone read the findings, and the security team wants images like that stopped earlier. Images with critical vulnerabilities must be stopped in the build stage, before they are pushed to the registry. Developers must get a vulnerability report in the pipeline so they can fix the image without opening another tool. Which change should the solutions architect make?
options: Keep ECR enhanced scanning on push and add an EventBridge rule that emails the security team when critical findings appear.
Enable Security Hub CSPM controls for Amazon ECR and review the failed controls before each release reaches production.
Add an Amazon Inspector CI/CD image scan to the build stage and fail the build when critical vulnerabilities are reported.
Turn on GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for the ECS clusters so that exploited vulnerabilities are detected in production containers.
questions.correct_rationale: Inspector CI/CD scanning reports vulnerabilities inside the pipeline, so the build can fail before the image is pushed.
distractor_rationales: Scanning on push happens after the image is in the registry, which the first requirement rules out.
CSPM controls check registry configuration, not the vulnerabilities inside each image during the build.
Runtime Monitoring detects threats after deployment, not vulnerabilities before the push.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is after push; WB is runtime; X checks configuration.

questions.subdomain: 5.3 Design observability and monitoring solutions
questions.question: A media company runs about 60 workload accounts in one organization, and its central operations team troubleshoots incidents that span several accounts. Engineers switch roles from account to account to compare metrics, logs, and traces, which slows every incident. A previous project that copied logs into a central bucket became costly and still lacked metrics and traces. Operators must search metrics, logs, and traces from all workload accounts in one place without copying the data. Accounts added to the workload OUs must join the central view with no step for the operations team. What should the solutions architect set up?
options: Stream metrics from each workload account to the operations account through metric streams and query them in Athena.
Create an audit role in each workload account and give operators a list of role links to switch between accounts faster.
Create log subscription filters in every workload account that stream log events through Firehose to a bucket in the operations account.
Make the operations account a CloudWatch monitoring account and link the workload OUs as source accounts that share their telemetry.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-account observability lets a monitoring account view source-account data in place, and OU-based linking covers new accounts.
distractor_rationales: Metric streams copy metrics and miss logs and traces, which the first requirement rules out.
Role switching keeps the account-by-account process and gives no single place to search.
Subscription filters copy logs and leave out metrics and traces, which the first requirement rules out.
questions.distractor_summary: WA copies logs only; WB has no single view; X copies metrics only.

questions.subdomain: 5.3 Design observability and monitoring solutions
questions.question: The on-call engineer for an online grocery service was paged more than 40 times during one incident because separate alarms for latency, errors, and queue depth each sent notifications. Reviews show that customers are affected when error rate and latency are high together, while either one alone usually clears by itself. The on-call engineer must be paged when the error alarm and the latency alarm are both in alarm. The individual alarms must stay in place for dashboards and investigation, but must stop paging on their own. Which change should the solutions architect make?
options: Delete the latency alarm and keep paging on the error alarm, because the error rate usually rises when customers are affected.
Raise the evaluation periods on the error and latency alarms so each one waits longer before it sends a page to on-call.
Create a composite alarm whose rule requires both child alarms in alarm, page from it, and remove paging from the children.
Add an SNS subscription filter policy so that on-call receives pages from the error alarm and drops pages from the latency alarm.
questions.correct_rationale: A composite alarm combines child alarm states in a rule, so it can page when both are in alarm while children stay silent.
distractor_rationales: Deleting the latency alarm removes it from dashboards, which the second requirement rules out.
Longer evaluation still pages from each alarm separately, which the first requirement rules out.
Filtering drops latency pages but still pages on errors alone, not on both together.
questions.distractor_summary: WA pages separately; WB pages on errors alone; X loses an alarm.

questions.subdomain: 5.3 Design observability and monitoring solutions
questions.question: A regional bank's online banking site has almost no traffic between midnight and six in the morning. Twice this year a deployment late at night broke the login page, and the problem was found by the first customers who logged in the next morning, long after the overnight on-call engineer could have fixed it. A broken login flow must be detected during the night even when no customers are using the site. The check must exercise the login steps a customer follows, not just confirm that the servers respond. What should the solutions architect add?
options: Create a CloudWatch Synthetics canary that scripts the login steps on a schedule and alarms to on-call when it fails.
Analyze the load balancer access logs each night and alarm to on-call when the number of failed login requests rises.
Add CloudWatch RUM to the login page so that browser errors from customer sessions raise an alarm to on-call overnight.
Rely on the load balancer target health checks for the web servers and alarm to on-call when targets become unhealthy.
questions.correct_rationale: A canary performs the customer's login steps on a schedule, so failures appear even without customer traffic.
distractor_rationales: Access logs need real login attempts, and there are almost none at night.
RUM collects data from real customer sessions, which are absent overnight.
Target health checks confirm a server responds, not that the login flow works.
questions.distractor_summary: WA and WB need customers; X checks servers.

questions.subdomain: 5.4 Design operational automation and resilient systems
questions.question: A manufacturer must rotate an agent configuration on EC2 instances in every account of two production OUs across three Regions after a vendor advisory. Last time, engineers signed in to each account and Region and ran the same runbook, which took four days and left several accounts missed. The next advisory is expected soon. The runbook must be started once from the central operations account against both OUs and all three Regions. The run must limit how many accounts change at once and stop when errors pass a set threshold. Which approach should the solutions architect use?
options: Use Run Command in the central account to target instances in the production accounts directly by their instance IDs.
Give engineers a checklist of accounts and Regions so they sign in to each one and run the runbook in order.
Deploy a Lambda function to every account through a StackSet that runs the runbook locally at a scheduled time in each Region.
Start one multi-account Automation execution that targets both OUs and Regions, with concurrency and error limits configured.
questions.correct_rationale: Multi-account automation runs one runbook across OUs and Regions from a central account with concurrency and error controls.
distractor_rationales: Run Command in one account does not target instances in other accounts by ID.
Signing in to each account repeats the slow manual process that missed accounts last time.
Scheduled local runs are not started centrally and give no shared concurrency or error threshold.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is uncoordinated; WB is manual; X cannot reach other accounts.

questions.subdomain: 5.4 Design operational automation and resilient systems
questions.question: A ticketing platform's web tier runs in an Auto Scaling group with target tracking on CPU. Traffic rises sharply every weekday morning, and new instances need about 10 minutes to warm their caches, so users see slow pages for the first part of each rush. The morning start time also shifts with school terms and holidays. Capacity must be in service before the recurring morning rise instead of after CPU climbs. Capacity must follow the shifting start time without the team editing schedules, and must not stay high all day. Which change should the solutions architect make?
options: Add scheduled actions that raise the minimum size each weekday morning and update the times whenever terms and holidays change.
Add a predictive scaling policy that forecasts load and launches ahead of it, and keep target tracking for unexpected spikes.
Replace target tracking with step scaling that adds larger groups of instances as soon as CPU passes each threshold.
Lower the target tracking CPU target so the group scales out sooner and keeps more spare instances running throughout the day.
questions.correct_rationale: Predictive scaling launches capacity before forecasted load, and target tracking still reacts to unexpected changes.
distractor_rationales: Scheduled actions need the team to edit times as the start shifts, which the second requirement rules out.
Step scaling is still reactive and starts after CPU has climbed.
A lower target keeps extra capacity all day and is still reactive.
questions.distractor_summary: WA needs schedule edits; WB stays high and reactive; X is reactive.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design architectures built for the cloud
questions.question: An order platform writes order events to an SQS queue, and a fulfillment workflow in Step Functions must start for each order. A Lambda function now sits in the middle: it polls the queue, drops test orders, calls an internal pricing API to add customer tier data, and starts the workflow, and the team maintains about four hundred lines of glue code for it. Test orders must be discarded before they reach the workflow, and each real order must carry customer tier data from the pricing API. The team wants to retire the custom polling and routing code and keep a point-to-point integration from the queue to the workflow. Which design should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Keep the Lambda poller but move its filter and pricing logic into a shared layer so the glue code is reused across other teams.
Send the order events to an EventBridge event bus with a rule that targets the state machine, and add the tier data in the first state.
Create an EventBridge pipe from the queue to the state machine with a filter for test orders and an enrichment call to the pricing API.
Create an EventBridge pipe from the queue to the state machine and let the workflow discard test orders and call the pricing API itself.
questions.correct_rationale: A pipe gives a point-to-point source-to-target integration with built-in filtering and an enrichment step, so no custom poller is needed.
distractor_rationales: Keeping the Lambda poller keeps the custom code the team wants to retire.
An event bus rule needs a producer change, and adding tier data in the workflow lets test orders through unfiltered.
Moving the filtering and enrichment into the workflow means test orders still start executions, which the first requirement rules out.
questions.distractor_summary: WA skips the filter; WB keeps the code; X uses a bus without filtering.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design architectures built for the cloud
questions.question: A brokerage processes account updates such as deposits, withdrawals, and transfers from a single SQS FIFO queue. All messages use the same message group ID, so one slow account blocks every other account and the backlog grows during market open, even though updates for different accounts have no ordering relationship with each other. Updates for the same account must still be processed in the order they were sent. Updates for different accounts must be processed in parallel so one slow account does not delay the others. What change should the solutions architect make?
options: Create a separate FIFO queue for each new account and add a router function that forwards every update to the matching queue.
Keep the FIFO queue and set the message group ID to the account ID so each account forms its own ordered group within the queue.
Keep the FIFO queue with one shared message group ID and raise the consumer batch size so more updates are read in each poll.
Move the updates to an SQS standard queue and scale the consumers out so different accounts are processed at the same time.
questions.correct_rationale: Message groups keep ordering within each group while different groups are processed in parallel within one FIFO queue.
distractor_rationales: Per-account queues and a router add operational overhead that message groups already avoid within one queue.
A single shared group still serializes every account, which the second requirement rules out.
A standard queue drops the per-account ordering that the first requirement keeps.
questions.distractor_summary: WA keeps one group; WB loses ordering; X adds queues and a router.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design architectures built for the cloud
questions.question: A ticketing company runs its checkout API on Lambda behind API Gateway. Every weekday at noon a sale opens and traffic jumps within seconds, and the first wave of buyers sees slow responses while new execution environments initialize. Outside the sale window traffic is light, and finance has asked the team not to pay for warm capacity that sits idle overnight. Checkout responses during the noon sale must not suffer initialization delays. Warm capacity must not be paid for outside the predictable sale window. Which approach meets these needs?
options: Set provisioned concurrency on the function alias and use Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions to raise it before noon.
Raise the reserved concurrency on the function so the sale traffic cannot be throttled by other functions in the account.
Configure a fixed level of provisioned concurrency on the function alias that stays in place around the clock for the sale peak.
Add an EventBridge rule that invokes the function every minute before noon to keep a few execution environments warm.
questions.correct_rationale: Provisioned concurrency removes initialization delay, and scheduled scaling matches it to the predictable noon window.
distractor_rationales: Reserved concurrency caps and guarantees concurrency but does not pre-initialize environments, so cold starts remain.
Fixed provisioned concurrency pays for warm capacity overnight, which the second requirement rules out.
A ping rule keeps a handful of environments warm and cannot cover a sudden jump to many concurrent buyers.
questions.distractor_summary: WA pays all day; WB keeps cold starts; X warms too few.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.2 Integrate AI and ML services into architectures
questions.question: A property firm hosts a small CPU-based valuation model on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that runs all day. Agents call it in short bursts during open houses on weekends and rarely during the week, and the endpoint shows near-zero utilization for most hours. The model runs on CPU and needs no access to resources inside a VPC. The team wants to stop paying for an endpoint that sits idle between bursts of requests. Agents accept a slower first response after an idle period, as long as later requests in the burst are quick. Which hosting option should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Move the model to a SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference endpoint that queues each request and writes its result to an S3 bucket.
Move the model to an on-demand SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint that scales with bursts and tolerates cold starts.
Run the model as a SageMaker AI batch transform job each weekend morning and serve agents the stored valuations from S3.
Keep a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on a smaller instance type so the idle hours cost less while responses stay warm all day.
questions.correct_rationale: On-demand Serverless Inference suits idle periods between spurts and accepts cold starts, which matches both needs.
distractor_rationales: Asynchronous Inference is designed for large payloads and long processing, and adds a queue and S3 result step agents do not need.
Batch transform precomputes results and cannot answer an agent's ad hoc request for a new property.
A smaller real-time instance still bills for every idle hour, which the first requirement rules out.
questions.distractor_summary: WA keeps idle cost; WB cannot serve ad hoc; X is for large payloads.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.2 Integrate AI and ML services into architectures
questions.question: A medical imaging startup runs a segmentation model on scanned studies that are several hundred megabytes each. Processing a study takes several minutes, and radiologists want results within a short time of upload rather than the next day. Requests arrive unevenly, and the current real-time endpoint times out on the largest studies. Each request carries a large payload and needs several minutes of processing without timing out. Results must come back in near real time after upload rather than in a nightly run. Which inference option should the solutions architect choose?
options: Keep the real-time endpoint and split each study into small chunks that the client sends as separate synchronous requests.
Deploy the model to an on-demand SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint so capacity scales with the uneven arrivals.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference endpoint that queues each study and writes the output to an S3 location.
Run a SageMaker AI batch transform job every night over the studies uploaded that day and notify the radiologists by email in the morning.
questions.correct_rationale: Asynchronous Inference queues large requests with long processing and returns results in near real time.
distractor_rationales: Chunking a scan for synchronous calls breaks the model input and still risks timeouts on processing time.
Serverless Inference is meant for short, bursty requests and does not handle multi-minute processing of large payloads.
A nightly batch job delays results to the next day, which the second requirement rules out.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is nightly; WB breaks input; X is for short requests.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design hybrid cloud integration patterns
questions.question: A logistics company connects twelve warehouses on three continents to a VPC in one Region with Site-to-Site VPN connections that terminate on a virtual private gateway. Enable acceleration on the existing Site-to-Site VPN connections that terminate on the virtual private gateway for each warehouse.
Attach the VPC to a transit gateway and create accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connections from each warehouse to that transit gateway.
Deploy a software VPN appliance on EC2 in the Region and point a Global Accelerator standard accelerator at the appliance's Elastic IP.
questions.correct_rationale: Accelerated VPN uses Global Accelerator edge entry and is supported for connections attached to a transit gateway.
distractor_rationales: Direct Connect adds dedicated circuits, which the second requirement rules out.
Virtual private gateways do not support accelerated connections, so the change cannot be made in place.
A self-managed appliance behind an accelerator adds operational burden and is not the managed accelerated VPN feature.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design hybrid cloud integration patterns
questions.question: A mining company runs containerized sensor analytics at remote sites whose satellite links drop for hours at a time. The platform team already runs Amazon EKS in a Region and wants the remote clusters to use the same Kubernetes tooling and EKS distribution, but each site must keep scheduling and running pods while its link is down. The remote clusters must keep operating through long disconnections from AWS. The remote clusters should use the EKS Kubernetes distribution and tooling the team already knows. Which option should the solutions architect recommend for the remote sites?

Run the sensor analytics as ECS tasks in the Region and send the sensor data over the satellite link for processing in AWS.
Install a self-managed upstream Kubernetes distribution at each site with its own tooling and add-ons maintained by the site staff.
Register the site servers as Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes in the Regional cluster so the EKS control plane in AWS manages each site.
questions.correct_rationale: EKS Anywhere runs the cluster locally and is the recommended option for disconnected or intermittent environments.

Upstream Kubernetes drops the EKS distribution and tooling the second requirement asks for.
Hybrid Nodes rely on a reliable connection to the Regional control plane, which the first requirement rules out.
questions.distractor_summary: WA needs a reliable link; WB drops EKS tooling; X stops offline.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design hybrid cloud integration patterns
questions.question: A semiconductor fab runs process-control software that reads from equipment controllers on the factory floor with single-digit millisecond latency. The company wants to manage this software with the same EC2 APIs, AMIs, and tooling it uses in its Region, but round trips from the fab to the nearest Region take far longer than the controllers allow. The software must run within the fab so it stays close to the equipment controllers and their data. The team must manage it with the same AWS APIs and tooling it uses in the Region. Run the process-control software on a private virtualization cluster in the fab and manage it with the existing on-site hypervisor tools.
Move the process-control instances to the nearest AWS Local Zone and connect the fab to it with a Site-to-Site VPN connection.
Install an AWS Outposts rack in the fab and run the process-control instances on it with the same EC2 APIs and AMIs used in the Region.
questions.correct_rationale: Outposts brings AWS infrastructure and APIs on premises for low-latency workloads near local data and applications.
distractor_rationales: Running in the Region keeps the long round trip that the first requirement rules out, even over Direct Connect.
An on-site hypervisor cluster loses the AWS APIs and tooling the second requirement asks for.
A Local Zone is still outside the fab and adds network distance to the controllers.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.4 Design network architectures
questions.question: A global retailer is replacing peered transit gateways in five Regions with AWS Cloud WAN. Payment card VPCs must be isolated from general corporate VPCs everywhere, while both groups need to reach a shared inspection VPC in each Region. The network team wants one policy document to express this instead of route tables edited by hand in each Region. Payment card VPCs and corporate VPCs must not exchange routes with each other in any Region. Both groups must reach the shared inspection VPC, with the intent written in one central policy. How should the solutions architect design the core network?
options: Keep the peered transit gateways and edit each route table by hand to send payment and corporate traffic to the inspection VPC.
Put all VPCs in separate segments and share routes between every pair of segments so each group can also reach the inspection VPC.
Put payment and corporate VPCs in separate Cloud WAN segments and use segment actions in the policy to share inspection routes.
Put payment and corporate VPCs in one Cloud WAN segment and block traffic between them with security groups in every Region.
questions.correct_rationale: Separate segments isolate routing domains, and segment actions in one policy share only the inspection routes.
distractor_rationales: Hand-edited route tables in each Region lose the single central policy the second requirement asks for.
Sharing routes between every pair of segments would also connect payment and corporate VPCs.
One shared segment exchanges routes between the groups, which the first requirement rules out.
questions.distractor_summary: WA shares a segment; WB is manual per Region; X shares everything.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.4 Design network architectures
questions.question: A bank runs dozens of microservices across many VPCs and accounts, some on EKS and some on Lambda. Teams now build VPC peering and internal load balancers for each new consumer, and the security team has asked that the payments service accept requests solely from the checkout service's IAM role, while other services remain open to any authenticated caller in the organization. Service-to-service traffic across VPCs and accounts must work without building peering or load balancers for each consumer. The payments service needs a stricter access rule than the rest, based on the caller's IAM identity. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Associate the VPCs and services with a VPC Lattice service network and rely on a single auth policy for the whole service network.
Expose each service through its own PrivateLink endpoint service and allow each consumer account on the endpoint service settings.
Associate the VPCs and services with a VPC Lattice service network and attach a stricter auth policy to the payments service.
Create VPC peering between each consumer VPC and the payments VPC and restrict access with security group rules for each caller.
questions.correct_rationale: A service network connects services across VPCs and accounts, and a service-level auth policy adds a stricter IAM rule for payments.
distractor_rationales: A single network-level policy cannot express the stricter rule for one service, which the second requirement asks for.
Per-service endpoint services still need setup for each consumer and do not check the caller's IAM role.
Peering for each consumer is the per-connection work the first requirement wants to avoid.
questions.distractor_summary: WA has one policy; WB uses peering; X lacks IAM checks.

questions.domain: 1. Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud
questions.subdomain: 1.4 Design network architectures
questions.question: A gaming company runs UDP game servers behind Network Load Balancers in three Regions. Console manufacturers require a short list of fixed IP addresses that they hardcode into allow lists, and players far from the Regions report high latency because their traffic crosses the public internet the whole way. Clients must use a small set of fixed IP addresses that do not change when Regional endpoints change. Player traffic must enter the AWS network near the player and reach the closest healthy Region. Which solution should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create a Global Accelerator custom routing accelerator and map each player to a fixed game server port in the nearest Region.
Assign Elastic IP addresses to each NLB and publish all of them to partners with Route 53 latency-based records for the game domain.
Create a Global Accelerator standard accelerator with the NLBs in each Region as endpoints and give partners its anycast static IPs.
Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the NLBs and give partners the IP ranges that CloudFront edge locations use.

distractor_rationales: Blanket denies block all creation instead of checking compliance, and halt delivery.

Detective controls still flag after deployment, which the first requirement rules out.

distractor_rationales: Storage Lens reports usage and activity metrics, not whether objects contain personal data.

Run an antivirus fleet on EC2 that polls the upload bucket and copies clean files to a second bucket used for ingestion.
Enable GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 on the upload bucket and ingest objects whose scan result tag marks them clean.
Add a Bedrock guardrail to the assistant so harmful content in retrieved passages is filtered from responses given to staff.

distractor_rationales: S3 Protection watches API activity and does not scan object content for malware.
A self-run antivirus fleet is the maintained servers the second requirement rules out.
A guardrail filters model input and output text and does not detect malware in uploaded files.

Ask the application developers to write prompts and responses to a DynamoDB table when they remember to add logging code.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Design architectures based on AWS pricing models
questions.question: A retailer runs its loyalty database on RDS for MySQL as one large Single-AZ instance in a memory-optimized instance class, and the finance team bought a size-flexible reserved DB instance for it last quarter. An outage review now asks for a standby in a second Availability Zone, and the cost analyst has drafted several ways to make the change. Move to a Multi-AZ deployment on two medium instances in the same class and switch the engine to PostgreSQL to cut licence spend.
Move to a Multi-AZ deployment on two medium instances in a general purpose class so the reservation follows the smaller size.
Move to a Multi-AZ deployment on two medium instances in the same memory-optimized class, engine, and Region as the reservation.

questions.question: A ticketing company expects a sharp spike for a two-week concert presale and must run a fixed number of large compute instances in one Availability Zone that hosts a latency-sensitive cache cluster. questions.subdomain: 3.2 Optimize data transfer and network costs
questions.question: A streaming publisher serves video segments to viewers on several continents through a CloudFront distribution in front of a packaging origin hosted in one Region. Run a fleet of reverse caching proxies on EC2 in front of the origin and point the distribution at the proxy load balancer.
Enable Origin Shield on the origin in the Region closest to it so regional edge caches share one extra caching layer.

Adding the country to the cache key splits the cache and lowers the hit ratio.
A self-run proxy fleet is the extra caching tier that the second requirement rules out.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Optimize data transfer and network costs

Keep cross-zone load balancing off and lower the health check interval so hot targets are marked unhealthy sooner.

With cross-zone off, each node still sends traffic to targets in its own zone, so the first requirement is not met.
Adding targets to balance the zones changes the per-zone target count that the second requirement keeps.

questions.subdomain: 3.3 Design cost allocation and visibility solutions

questions.subdomain: 3.4 Optimize storage and database costs

Add a pipeline stage that pushes each image to repositories in every workload account and Region after the build step succeeds.

A table of hourly thresholds must be maintained by hand, which the second requirement rules out.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design architectures built for the cloud
